'''William Edward Story''' (April 29, 1850 – April 10, 1930) was an American [[mathematician]] who taught at [[Johns Hopkins University]] and [[Clark University]].

William was born in Boston to Isaac Marion Story (1818-1901) and Elizabeth Bowen Woodberry (1817-1888). He attended high school in Somerville, Massachusetts, and entered [[Harvard University]] in the fall of 1867. He graduated with honors in mathematics and began graduate study in [[Germany]] in September 1871.<ref>''Who Was Who in America'', Volume I, 1897-1942, p. 1195.</ref> In [[Berlin]] he attended lectures of [[Weierstrass]], [[Ernst Kummer]], [[Helmholtz]] and Dove. In [[Leipzig]] he heard [[Karl Neumann (mathematician)|Karl Neumann]], Bruhns, Mayer, Van der Müll, and Engelmann. He earned a Ph.D. in Leipzig in 1875 with a dissertation ''On the algebraic relations existing between the polars of a binary quantic''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=William Story - The Mathematics Genealogy Project |url=https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=7451 |access-date=2025-11-20 |website=www.mathgenealogy.org}}</ref>

W.E. Story began his teaching career at Harvard as a [[tutor]]. With the establishment of [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1876, Story was recruited by [[Daniel Coit Gilman]] as an Associate.  [[J. J. Sylvester]] led the program in mathematics. Until 1879, Story was the only other instructor in mathematics besides Sylvester.<ref>Hugh Hawkins (1960) ''Pioneer: A History of the Johns Hopkins University, 1874-1889'', page 135.</ref>  Story was instrumental in starting two publication projects: ''The Johns Hopkins University Circulars'' was a student paper detailing classes and attendees. ''[[American Journal of Mathematics]]'' was also started as a joint effort of Sylvester and Story, but soon Story was replaced by [[Thomas Craig (mathematician)|Thomas Craig]] as managing editor. In 1893, Story became an [[associate professor]]; he taught courses on [[quaternions]], [[elliptic function]]s, [[invariant theory]], mathematical astronomy and mathematical elasticity. Story also introduced introductory courses for graduate students, surveying the entire field. The monthly Mathematical Seminary became a weekly mathematical society, divided into three parts; Story oversaw the section on geometry and quaternions.<ref>Hawkins, pp. 137-138.</ref>

When [[Clark University]] was established in 1889, President [[G. Stanley Hall]] hired [[Oskar Bolza]] and Story to lead the mathematics department.<ref>W. E. Story (1899) [https://archive.org/details/clarkuniversi00stor Clark University 1889–1899, a decennial celebration] from [[Internet Archive]]</ref> [[Henry Taber]] was hired as [[docent]], he had studied with Story at Johns Hopkins.<ref>Hawkins, p. 138,</ref> [[Solomon Lefschetz]] and other mathematicians contributed to making Clark the leading site for mathematics in the USA until 1892 when [[University of Chicago]] eclipsed it.<ref>Cooke, Roger and Rickey, V. Frederick (1989) "W.E. Story of Hopkins and Clark" in ''A Century of Mathematics in America'', Part III, [[Peter Duren]] and others, editors, [[American Mathematical Society]] pages 29–76, {{ISBN|0-8218-0130-9}}</ref>

Clark University ceased its graduate program in 1919 and Story retired in 1921. He died in 1930 in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2005 |title=William Edward Story |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Story/ |access-date=2025-11-20 |website=MacTutor}}</ref>
